name: TBCK-related intellectual disability syndrome
aliases: hypotonia, infantile, with psychomotor retardation and characteristic facies (IHPRF3)

clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TBCK, which encodes a protein implicated in the regulation of mTOR signalling and autophagy, so it is a metabolic-neurodegenerative disorder rather than a chromatin-modifier syndrome
Profound infantile hypotonia, global developmental delay and intellectual disability with a distinctive facial appearance are the core features
Many children have severe feeding and respiratory difficulty, and progressive, neurodegenerative decline can occur in more severely affected individuals
A recurrent founder variant is prevalent in individuals of Puerto Rican ancestry and is associated with a severe, progressive phenotype
Neuroimaging may show white matter abnormalities (leukoencephalopathy), a thin corpus callosum and brain atrophy
Epilepsy, hyporeflexia and features of a motor neuronopathy or neuropathy may develop over time
Diagnosis rests on identifying biallelic pathogenic TBCK variants, and inheritance is autosomal recessive with implications for carrier and reproductive counselling
reference.pathophysiology: TBCK encodes a multidomain protein carrying a TBC domain and a pseudokinase region that is thought to participate in regulating the mTOR signalling pathway and cellular autophagy, processes central to cell growth, protein turnover and the clearance of cellular waste. Biallelic loss-of-function variants reduce or abolish functional protein, dysregulating mTOR-related signalling and impairing autophagy so that abnormal material accumulates within cells, with some findings suggesting a lysosomal storage-like component. The nervous system is especially vulnerable, producing profound hypotonia, developmental impairment, white matter disease and, in severe cases, progressive neurodegeneration, while the severity varies with the specific genotype including the severe founder variant.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic causes of severe infantile hypotonia (e.g. spinal muscular atrophy)
Congenital myopathies and congenital muscular dystrophies
Prader-Willi syndrome and other causes of neonatal hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to identify biallelic TBCK variants, with targeted testing for the founder variant in relevant ancestries
Brain MRI to characterise leukoencephalopathy, corpus callosum thinning and atrophy
Assessment of feeding and swallowing with respiratory evaluation
Neuromuscular assessment including nerve conduction studies if a neuropathy is suspected
Creatine kinase and metabolic screening to help exclude alternative diagnoses
redFlags: Respiratory insufficiency or recurrent aspiration requiring urgent support
Developmental regression or loss of skills indicating progression
Severe feeding failure with faltering growth
Rapid neurological deterioration in the severe (founder-variant) phenotype
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely with genotype: milder cases have static severe developmental impairment, whereas the severe form, including the founder variant, is often progressive with neurodegeneration, respiratory compromise and shortened survival; care is supportive, centring on feeding, respiratory management, seizure control and developmental support.
pitfalls: Overlooking the recurrent founder variant in individuals of Puerto Rican ancestry
Mistaking the disorder for a static encephalopathy and missing its potential to progress
Attributing the hypotonia to a primary neuromuscular disease without genetic testing
Failing to provide recurrence-risk counselling appropriate to autosomal recessive inheritance
Underestimating respiratory risk that drives much of the morbidity
references: Nature Reviews — mTOR signalling, autophagy and neurodevelopmental disease
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying therapy, so management is supportive and directed at the neurological, feeding and respiratory manifestations
Support feeding and nutrition with swallowing assessment and gastrostomy where oral intake is unsafe
Provide respiratory care including secretion management, prompt infection treatment and ventilatory support as decline progresses
Manage hypotonia and developmental impairment with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy
Control epilepsy with anticonvulsant therapy where seizures occur
Monitor for neurodegenerative progression and involve palliative care in severe, progressive disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric care across neurology, respiratory and allied health
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with targeted founder-variant testing in Puerto Rican families and carrier testing of relatives
